The racing line
Why the fastest way round a track is almost always the shortest and the smoothest.
Takeaway
Slow down, make it short, make it smooth, then add speed.

Cars and drones
Car racers have a racing line too. A car wants to go straight, and so does a drone.
in: start wide
apex: kiss the inside
out: wide again
a car: fights the grip of the road
a drone: no edges, only the ground
up and down are part of the line: climbing costs speed, diving gives it back
1
Both want to go straight
Every change of direction costs speed. On a drone you can hear it: the props squeal.
2
No edges
A drone has no road edges, only gates and the ground. The short line is open.
3
Up and down count
The line is 3D. Height costs and gives speed, like a roller coaster.
Free to use in your own trainings. Just tell people where you got it.

Step 1: slow down
Too fast for your skill? Slow down first. A fast lap only counts if you can fly it every lap.
Pushing too hard
fast lap
crash, restart
missed gate, go back
Fast and clean
clean lap
clean lap
clean lap
finished
still flying
1
Clean beats fast
Three clean laps beat one fast lap and two crashes.
2
Missed gates cost
Going back for a gate costs far more than flying it a little slower.
3
Slow it down
Is a section going wrong? Fly it slower and smoother. Lap times often drop.

Step 2: make it short
Wide lines add distance. Over a full course, the fastest pilots can fly less than half the distance a novice does.
Novice
Lines up on every gate, overshoots, swings wide. Misses one gate and goes back for it.
Fast pilot
Turns early, cuts close to every gate. Short, smooth, full speed.
Distance flown in one lap

The pre-turn: already face the exit as you go through the gate.
Turn after the gate
Straight through, then brake, turn and line up again. Long, and slow out of the gate.
Pre-turn

Look one or more gates ahead
Your line starts with your eyes. Good pilots already look at the next gate.
eyes here: the next gate
the gate you are flying through
what you see in the goggles
1.5 s
Pilots first look at a gate about 1.5 seconds before they reach it: about 16 m ahead.
0.2 s
The eyes move first. The hands follow about 0.2 seconds later.
Late = crash
Before a crash, pilots looked at the gate later than on clean laps. Look at the inside of the turn.

Three ways to see a track
As you get better, you see less of the track. That is the point.
1 · Magnetic gates
Every gate pulls you in, and so does anything else in the field: a branch, a tree. One gate at a time, then look for the next.
you hit what you look at
2 · Gates become flags
You only worry about the post that matters, not the whole gate. Your head has room for the line.
only the post that matters
3 · Flow
You only see your line. The gates may as well not be there. Nothing extra left to think about.
only the line
It’s a step up in skill, and it’s also getting rid of what you don’t need.
Free to use in your own trainings. Just tell people where you got it.

16 · The racing line · fig. 9
Step 3: make it smooth
Smooth means you slow down and speed up less often. Throttle high and steady, fewer, rounder inputs.
throttle
roll stick
Rough: brake, speed up, correct
Every chop of the throttle loses speed. Every stab on the sticks needs a correction.
throttle
roll stick
Smooth: high throttle, one input, held
The drone keeps its speed. One round input does the whole turn.
1
Less braking
You slow down and speed up less often. Speed you keep is time you save.
2
Less propwash
Chopping the throttle drops the drone into its own dirty air. Steady throttle keeps it clean.
3
Less turning round
Less time spent pointing the drone a new way. That is what flow feels like.
Free to use in your own trainings. Just tell people where you got it.

Even champions have time to find
Researchers in Zurich let a computer plan the perfect line and raced it against two expert pilots.
Computer line
6.12 s
Expert pilot 1
6.79 s
Expert pilot 2
6.99 s
best lap on the same track: shorter is faster
About 10 % faster
The perfect line beat the best human laps by about 10 %.
Ten times steadier
The computer’s laps varied by hundredths of a second, the pilots’ by tenths.
Why?
Pilots plan a gate or two ahead and don’t hold full power all the way round. So there is always time to find.
